prompt: Make a chart of monthly rainfall for the town of Quillon: Jan 82mm, Feb 64, Mar 71, Apr 55, May 48, Jun 31, Jul 18, Aug 22, Sep 47, Oct 89, Nov 112, Dec 104. It's for a gardening club newsletter. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: The chart form fits a month-by-month series (bars or a line) and is easy to read.
The value axis starts at zero if bars are used.
Months are in calendar order and labeled legibly.
There is a plain title and units (mm) are stated.
Color is restrained and not a rainbow; the wettest months may be called out with direct labels.

prompt: We made a pie chart with 11 slices for our nonprofit's annual spend by program: Meals 38%, Shelter 21%, Legal aid 9%, Youth 8%, Job training 7%, Health 5%, Outreach 4%, Admin 3%, Fundraising 2%, Events 2%, Other 1%. It uses a rainbow legend. Board members complain they can't read it. What should we do instead?
rubric: Identifies too many slices and legend lookup as the core problem.
Recommends a sorted horizontal bar chart or equivalent ranking form.
Suggests direct labels with values instead of a color legend.
Suggests grouping or muting minor items without hiding them.
Gives enough specifics to implement.

prompt: We want to show whether our app's weekly active users (in thousands) are growing: 41, 43, 42, 47, 52, 51, 58, 61, 60, 66, 71, 75 over twelve weeks. Should it be a bar chart, a line chart or an area chart? And should the y axis start at zero?
rubric: Recommends a line or equally appropriate form for a time trend and justifies it.
Addresses axis baseline honestly, noting that a line chart can use a non-zero baseline but bars cannot.
Mentions labeling the first and last values or key points.
Answers both questions directly.

prompt: Create a chart comparing three regional sales teams' quarterly revenue ($ thousands) across four quarters: North 410, 455, 430, 520; South 380, 372, 410, 395; West 290, 340, 365, 480. The audience is executives; they care about who grew most. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: Chart type allows comparing each team's trajectory (lines or small multiples, or clearly grouped bars).
Series are identified with direct labels near the lines/bars rather than only a distant legend.
Axes include units ($K) and time labels.
The team that grew most is made evident through emphasis or annotation.
At most a few restrained colors are used, distinguishable beyond hue alone.

prompt: This SVG bar chart needs cleaning up. It has: a 3D effect, a gradient fill on bars, gridlines in black every 10 units, a legend for a single series, a y axis running 40-100 for values 52, 61, 58, 90 labeled 'Q1'..'Q4', and a title 'Chart'. Produce an improved version as one HTML file with inline SVG or canvas, no external assets.
rubric: Removes the 3D effect and gradient for flat solid marks.
The y axis baseline begins at zero.
Gridlines become light or are removed, and the single-series legend is removed.
The title says what the chart shows.
Bars have direct value labels or a clear axis.

prompt: Explain to a new analyst why a dual-axis chart showing our ad spend (left axis, $) and signups (right axis, count) can mislead, and what to do instead. Keep it practical.
rubric: Explains that axis scaling choices can manufacture or hide a correlation.
Offers at least two alternatives such as separate stacked panels, indexed values or a scatter plot.
Gives a concrete example based on the stated variables.
Stays brief and applied.

prompt: Show how ticket prices for a rail line vary by distance. Data: 5 km $2.10, 10 km $3.40, 20 km $5.80, 40 km $9.20, 80 km $14.50, 160 km $21.00. Also a short note saying fares are capped at 160 km. Provide a single HTML page with inline SVG, no external assets.
rubric: The chart handles uneven distance spacing honestly (scatter/line on a true or clearly labeled scale).
Axes labeled with units (km, $).
Data points are marked and a few key values are labeled directly.
The cap note is attached to the relevant part of the chart.
Visual design is minimal, with no chart junk.

prompt: A teammate made a simple bar chart of survey results: 'Satisfied' 72%, 'Neutral' 19%, 'Unsatisfied' 9% for a clinic. It's a clean horizontal bar chart, sorted in that order, bars in one blue color, percentage labels at bar ends, a zero baseline, a clear title. Anything to fix?
rubric: Recognizes the chart is already good and says so.
Does not recommend replacing it with a different form.
If offering changes, they are small (e.g., sample size note).
Answer is brief.

prompt: For a quick internal note, I have two numbers: our median delivery time was 3.2 days last year and 2.4 days this year. Do I need a chart? What would you show?
rubric: Considers that a chart may be unnecessary for two numbers and states a recommendation.
If a chart is proposed, it is a simple comparison with a zero baseline or just labeled numbers.
Mentions the change explicitly (e.g. 0.8 days faster, 25%).
Avoids elaborate or decorative treatments.

prompt: Make a small chart showing a marathon runner's pace per kilometer over 42 km, for her training log. Pace in min/km for km 1-42 starts at 5:05 and slowly rises to about 5:40 by km 42 with a spike to 6:10 at km 30 (a water stop). Generate plausible values. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: Line chart or equivalent over the kilometer axis with 42 points.
The y axis communicates that lower is faster, or is clearly labeled in min/km.
The km 30 spike is annotated directly.
Axis tick labels use a readable time format (m:ss) rather than raw decimals.
Minimal styling with no 3D or heavy gridlines.
